newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senators ask higher trade role for ag issues.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators ask higher trade role for ag issues.

text.p: Farm-state senators asked the Clinton administration Tuesday to give high priority to agriculture in trade discussion worldwide and especially with China, a booming market for U.S. farm products.

"The rest of the world needs to open up their markets or there will be great suffering. America's agricultural production is critical to feeding the entire world," Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Richard Lugar said in a statement.
Lugar, an Indiana Republican, said in his statement that acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in a face-to-face meeting that trade barriers to U.S. products must be removed.
Sixteen senators, including Lugar, sent a letter to President Clinton outlining 10 issues that must be settled to assure fair access to China's booming market for food.

"No market holds greater promise for U.S. food, feed and fiber exports than China," their letter said. "We believe it is critically important that agricultural concerns occupy a high priority as you administration engages the Chinese n discussions and negotiations."
Farm-trade disputes with Europe "must be resolved," Lugar said. He wants agriculture to be a centerpiece in trade talks.
Pending issues with the European Union include disagreement over sales of beef produced with synthetic growth hormones and so-called veterinary equivalency rules.

Farm issues with China include market access, limits on subsidies, disciplines on so-called state trading enterprises that can hold monopoly control on exports and imports, and whether China should be classed as a developing country or made subject to stricter rules for industrialized nations. U.S. ag exports to China were $2.6 billion in fiscal 1995 and projected to reach $4.6 billion in 2005.
